title: Which prompt sets real boundaries?
scenario: You are sending a product update to existing customers. Legal has rules: no client names, no promises about future releases.
task: Which prompt gives the useful boundaries?
promptA: Write a product update. Keep it short and professional and don't oversell.
promptB: Write a product update for existing customers: maximum 120 words, three short paragraphs (what changed, what it means for them, what to do next). No marketing adjectives; no client names; no promises about future releases.

feedback.a: “Short” and “don't oversell” are directions, not boundaries — nothing here is countable or checkable, and the legal rules are simply absent.
feedback.b: Length is a number, structure is a shape, and the exclusions name the exact failure modes. Every draft now fails specifically — and fixes in one edit.

hints: Count the things you could actually check in a review.
explanation: Constraints turn review from taste into a checklist: length, scope, must-keep, must-avoid. Given boundaries, you stop negotiating about “short” and start fixing the actual sentence that broke a rule.
